## SQL Functional Tests

This document contains functional tests for the SQL extension. The tests correspond to the feature matrix and cover client-side execution, static delivery, normal SQL blocks, editor options, isolated exercises, shared environments, setup and grading, error feedback, schema-aware autocomplete, psql-style meta commands, meta-command autocomplete, and autorun.

The tests are intended to be executed in the rendered HTML document. Unless stated otherwise, editable SQL blocks should be executed manually with **Run Code**.

## Test 1: Client-side SQL execution and static delivery

This test verifies that SQL statements can be executed in the browser through PGlite. The rendered HTML page is intended to be opened through a static local web server without an external SQL server.

#### Source

````{.markdown filename="sql-functional-test.qmd"}
```{sql}
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS functional_people;

CREATE TABLE functional_people (
  id INTEGER,
  name TEXT
);

INSERT INTO functional_people VALUES
  (1, 'Ada'),
  (2, 'Linus');
```

````

```{sql}
#| edit: true
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS functional_people;

CREATE TABLE functional_people (
  id INTEGER,
  name TEXT

);

INSERT INTO functional_people VALUES
  (1, 'Ada'),
  (2, 'Linus');
```

#### Source

````{.markdown filename="sql-functional-test.qmd"}
```{sql}

SELECT *
FROM functional_people
ORDER BY id;
```

````

```{sql}
SELECT *
FROM functional_people
ORDER BY id;
```

Expected result: After running the blocks in order, the second block displays two rows. The page can be rendered and executed through a static local web server without a Node, Quarto preview, or external SQL database server.

## Test 2: Normal SQL blocks, global state, tabular output, and before-all behavior

This test verifies that normal SQL blocks share a global database state. A table created in one normal SQL block should be available in later normal SQL blocks. This also demonstrates that a normal SQL block can function as a document-wide preparation step comparable to a limited before-all mechanism when executed before later blocks.

```{sql}
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS global_numbers;

CREATE TABLE global_numbers (
  id INTEGER,
  value INTEGER
);

INSERT INTO global_numbers VALUES
  (1, 10),
  (2, 20);
```

```{sql}
INSERT INTO global_numbers VALUES (3, 30);
```

```{sql}
SELECT
  id,
  value
FROM global_numbers
ORDER BY id;
```

Expected result: After running the blocks in order, the final SELECT output is displayed as a table with the columns `id` and `value` and contains three rows.

## Test 3: Isolated exercises

This test verifies that SQL exercises without a shared `envir` use separate database states. Two exercises use the same table name but should not interfere with each other.

```{sql}
#| exercise: isolated_one
#| setup: true

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS isolated_items;

CREATE TABLE isolated_items (
  id INTEGER,
  label TEXT
);

INSERT INTO isolated_items VALUES
  (1, 'first exercise setup');
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: isolated_one

INSERT INTO isolated_items VALUES
  (2, 'first exercise user row');

SELECT *
FROM isolated_items
ORDER BY id;
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: isolated_one
#| check: true

SELECT COUNT(*) = 2 AS passed
FROM isolated_items;
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: isolated_two
#| setup: true

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS isolated_items;

CREATE TABLE isolated_items (
  id INTEGER,
  label TEXT
);
INSERT INTO isolated_items VALUES
  (1, 'second exercise setup');
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: isolated_two

SELECT *
FROM isolated_items
ORDER BY id;
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: isolated_two
#| check: true

SELECT COUNT(*) = 1 AS passed
FROM isolated_items;
```

Expected result: The first exercise contains two rows after execution. The second exercise contains only its own setup row. This shows that the exercises do not accidentally share the same database state.

## Test 4: Shared environments

This test verifies that multiple exercises with the same `envir` option share one database state. The first exercise creates the table, and later exercises use and extend the same state.

```{sql}
#| exercise: shared_one
#| envir: shared_functional

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS shared_items;

CREATE TABLE shared_items (
  id INTEGER,
  label TEXT
);

INSERT INTO shared_items VALUES
  (1, 'created in first shared exercise');
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: shared_two
#| envir: shared_functional

INSERT INTO shared_items VALUES
  (2, 'created in second shared exercise');

SELECT *
FROM shared_items
ORDER BY id;
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: shared_three
#| envir: shared_functional

SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows
FROM shared_items;
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: shared_three
#| envir: shared_functional
#| check: true

SELECT COUNT(*) = 2 AS passed
FROM shared_items;
```

Expected result: After running the shared exercises in order, the shared environment contains both inserted rows. The check for `shared_three` passes because all exercises use the same `envir`.

## Test 5: Setup, grading, and error feedback

This test verifies that setup code prepares the exercise state, that check code evaluates the result, and that SQL errors are shown as feedback.

### Test 5.1: Correct grading result

```{sql}
#| exercise: grading_pass
#| setup: true

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS grading_numbers;

CREATE TABLE grading_numbers (
  value INTEGER
);
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: grading_pass

INSERT INTO grading_numbers VALUES
  (1),(2),(3);
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: grading_pass
#| check: true

SELECT COUNT(*) = 3 AS passed
FROM grading_numbers;
```

Expected result: The check passes because the table contains exactly three rows.

### Test 5.2: Negative grading result

```{sql}
#| exercise: grading_fail
#| setup: true

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS grading_fail_numbers;

CREATE TABLE grading_fail_numbers (
  value INTEGER
);
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: grading_fail

INSERT INTO grading_fail_numbers VALUES
  (1);
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: grading_fail
#| check: true

SELECT COUNT(*) = 3 AS passed
FROM grading_fail_numbers;
```

Expected result: The check fails because the table contains only one row instead of three.

### Test 5.3: SQL error feedback

```{sql}
#| exercise: grading_error
#| setup: true

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS grading_error_table;

CREATE TABLE grading_error_table (
  id INTEGER
);
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: grading_error

INSERT INTO table_that_does_not_exist VALUES (1);
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: grading_error
#| check: true

SELECT COUNT(*) = 1 AS passed
FROM grading_error_table;
```

Expected result: The SQL error is displayed as feedback and does not produce an uncaught browser error.

## Test 6: SQL editor, schema-aware autocomplete, and autorun

This test verifies editor-based SQL input, schema-aware autocomplete, and the Quarto Live editor option `autorun`.

### Test 6.1: Schema-aware autocomplete

This test verifies that the SQL editor can suggest table and column names from the current PGlite schema.

#### Source

````{.markdown filename="sql-functional-test.qmd"}
```{sql}
#| exercise: editor_autocomplete
#| setup: true

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS autocomplete_items;

CREATE TABLE autocomplete_items (
  id INTEGER,
  label TEXT,
  amount INTEGER
);

INSERT INTO autocomplete_items VALUES
  (1, 'first', 10),
  (2, 'second', 20);
```

````

```{sql}
#| exercise: editor_autocomplete
#| setup: true

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS autocomplete_items;

CREATE TABLE autocomplete_items (
  id INTEGER,
  label TEXT,
  amount INTEGER
);

INSERT INTO autocomplete_items VALUES
  (1, 'first', 10),
  (2, 'second', 20);
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: editor_autocomplete

SELECT
  id,
  label,
  amount
FROM autocomplete_items
ORDER BY id;
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: editor_autocomplete
#| check: true

SELECT COUNT(*) = 2 AS passed
FROM autocomplete_items;
```

Expected result: The SQL editor should suggest the table `autocomplete_items` and the columns `id`, `label`, and `amount`. The query should return two rows and the check should pass.

### Test 6.2: Autorun in SQL editor

This test verifies that an editable SQL block with `autorun: true` is executed automatically when the editor is initialized.

#### Source

````{.markdown filename="sql-functional-test.qmd"}
```{sql}
#| exercise: editor_autorun
#| autorun: true

INSERT INTO autorun_editor VALUES
  (1, 'created by editor autorun');

SELECT *
FROM autorun_editor;
```

````

```{sql}

#| setup: true

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS autorun_editor;

CREATE TABLE autorun_editor (
  id INTEGER,
  value TEXT
);
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: editor_autorun
#| autorun: true

INSERT INTO autorun_editor VALUES
  (1, 'created by editor autorun');

SELECT *
FROM autorun_editor;
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: editor_autorun
#| check: true

SELECT COUNT(*) = 1 AS passed
```

Expected result: The SQL block with `autorun: true` is executed automatically without pressing the run button. The output displays the inserted row and the check passes.

## Test 7: Editor option combinations

This test verifies the interaction between `edit` and `autorun`. The options affect different aspects of execution: `edit` controls whether an editor is shown, while `autorun` controls whether an editable block is executed automatically during initialization.

### Test 7.1: `edit: true`, `autorun: false`

This test verifies the default interactive editor behavior. The editor should be visible, but the SQL code should not be executed until **Run Code** is pressed.

```{sql}
#| edit: true
#| autorun: false

SELECT 'manual editor execution' AS mode;
```

Expected result: An editor is displayed. No result should be shown until **Run Code** is pressed. After execution, the output contains the value `manual editor execution`.

### Test 7.2: `edit: true`, `autorun: true`

This test verifies automatic execution of an editable non-exercise SQL block.

```{sql}
#| edit: true
#| autorun: true

SELECT 'automatic editor execution' AS mode;
```

Expected result: An editor is displayed and the SQL code is executed automatically during initialization. The output contains the value `automatic editor execution` without pressing **Run Code**.

### Test 7.3: `edit: false`, `autorun: false`

This test verifies non-editable SQL block behavior. Since the block is not editable, no editor should be shown. The block should be evaluated directly.

```{sql}
#| edit: false
#| autorun: false

SELECT 'direct evaluation without editor' AS mode;
```

Expected result: No editor is displayed. The output is shown directly and contains the value `direct evaluation without editor`.

### Test 7.4: `edit: false`, `autorun: true`

This test verifies that `edit: false` selects the non-interactive evaluation path. In this case, `autorun` is not the relevant trigger because no editor is created.

```{sql}
#| edit: false
#| autorun: true

SELECT 'direct evaluation ignores editor autorun' AS mode;
```

Expected result: No editor is displayed. The block is evaluated directly. The result contains the value `direct evaluation ignores editor autorun`.

## Test 8: Psql-style meta commands

This test verifies that psql-style meta commands are recognized by the SQL evaluator and executed through the current PGlite environment.

```{sql}
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS students;

CREATE TABLE students (
  id INTEGER,
  name TEXT
);

INSERT INTO students VALUES
  (1, 'Ada'),
  (2, 'Linus');
```

```{sql}
\?
```

```{sql}
\dt
```

```{sql}
\d students
```

```{sql}
\du
```

Expected result: The command `\?` displays help output. The command `\dt` lists the table `students`. The command `\d students` displays information about the columns of the table. The command `\du` is recognized as a supported meta command and returns the role information available in the current PGlite environment.

## Test 9: Meta commands and environments

This test verifies that meta commands use the same environment as regular SQL statements.

```{sql}
#| exercise: meta_env_create
#| envir: meta_shared

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS meta_students;
CREATE TABLE meta_students (
  id INTEGER,
  name TEXT
);

INSERT INTO meta_students VALUES
  (1, 'Ada');
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: meta_env_describe
#| envir: meta_shared

\d meta_students
```

```{sql}
#| exercise: meta_env_missing

\d meta_students
```

Expected result: The block with `envir: meta_shared` can describe the table `meta_students`, because the table was created in the same shared environment. The block without the shared `envir` does not see that table, because it uses a different exercise environment.

## Test 10: Meta-command autocomplete

This test verifies that the SQL editor suggests supported psql-style meta commands.

```{sql}
#| exercise: meta_command_completion
-- Type a backslash or "\d" in the editor and check whether meta commands
-- such as \?, \d, \dt, \du, \dg, \dn, \dv, \di, and \ds are suggested.
-- Delete these comments before execution

\dt
```

Expected result: When typing `\` or `\d` in the SQL editor, the editor suggests supported meta commands such as `\dt`, `\du`, and `\d`. Executing `\dt` runs the meta command through the SQL evaluator.

## Test 11: Meta commands as standalone input

This test documents the expected boundary of psql-style meta commands. Meta commands are treated as standalone inputs and should not be mixed with SQL statements in the same block.

```{sql}
#| edit: true
-- Execute this block as a normal SQL block.
-- Then execute meta commands such as \dt in a separate block.
-- Delete these comments before execution

SELECT 'meta commands should be executed separately' AS note;
```

Expected result: Regular SQL executes normally. Meta commands such as `\dt` should be used as separate editor input, not mixed with SQL statements in the same block.
